msgs.title: Being fully invested feels like wisdom in a rally.
msgs.pub:
Being fully invested feels like wisdom in a rally.

Ovid tells how King Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold.

The wish came true. Then he reached for bread and it turned to metal in his hand.

Retail near a top makes the same wish. Every dollar into the position.

It works for months. The account looks rich.

Then a bill arrives during a panic, and the only way to pay it is to sell at the low.

Cash looks dead in a rally. It is the bread.

Gold only counts if you can wait to sell it.

msgs.title: Your portfolio may still carry its names and none of its reasons.
msgs.pub:
Your portfolio may still carry its names and none of its reasons.

Plutarch tells of the ship of Theseus, kept by the Athenians for centuries.

Each rotten plank was replaced with a new one, until philosophers argued whether it was still the same ship.

Positions age the same way.

You bought for growth. Growth slowed, and now you hold for the dividend.

Every plank of the thesis has been swapped. The name on the hull stayed.

Fair enough, some theses should evolve.

Once a year I write each holding next to the reason I bought it. If the reason is gone, I judge it as a new buy at today's price.

msgs.title: Your sell rule is only as strong as your fear on the day you need it.
msgs.pub:
Your sell rule is only as strong as your fear on the day you need it.

Hume put it bluntly. Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions.

He meant that reason never moves us alone. It serves what we already want.

Watch a trader in a drawdown. The analysis keeps finding reasons to hold.

The fear of booking the loss writes the research.

I like to think I am the exception. My old trades disagree.

So I write the exit before the entry, while I want nothing yet.

That is the only hour my reason works for me.

msgs.title: Perma-bulls have an answer for every red day.
msgs.pub:
Perma-bulls have an answer for every red day.

Voltaire wrote a character for them in Candide.

Pangloss lives through disaster after disaster, the Lisbon earthquake included, and still says all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds.

Rates up, buy the dip. Earnings miss, buy it again.

Sometimes they are right. Dips have paid for years.

Then one day the dip is a new trend, and the explanation sounds exactly the same.

A thesis that explains every outcome tells you nothing.

I want to know in advance which price would prove me wrong.

msgs.title: High profits are the most public secret in markets.
msgs.pub:
High profits are the most public secret in markets.

Everyone can see them. That is the problem.

When a sector earns far more than normal, new money builds new capacity.

The supply shows up later, right when late bulls are paying the top multiple.

The price of the product falls. The margins drift back to normal.

The stock was priced for the peak to last forever.

When everyone agrees a business prints money, I start counting the new competitors.

msgs.pub:

Get me back to even and I am done.

Nobody keeps it.

Back at even, the account looks fine again, and fine feels like permission.

A few dollars up, and the old itch asks for one more trade.

That promise is a painkiller. It wears off the day the pain stops.

msgs.title: Most traders spend the day guessing what other traders will think.
msgs.pub:
Most traders spend the day guessing what other traders will think.

A number comes out. Before anyone reads it, funds are already betting on how retail will react.

Then retail bets on how funds will react to retail.

Nobody is trading the fact anymore.

That is how a good report sinks a stock by lunch.

There is no floor under a guess about a guess.

I try to start with what the business earns, before I think about anyone's reaction.
